Glossary — every term, simply Patta land Land for which a private owner holds a government-issued title record. Example: an ordinary farmer with a clean revenue record along the Musi’s middle reaches is a patta landowner under this scheme. Buffer zone A protective strip of land just outside a water body’s Full Tank Level, kept free of construction to protect its ecology and absorb flood flow. Example: land here gets 800 sq yards/acre under today’s scheme, less than ordinary patta land further from the river. Full Tank Level (FTL) The highest water level a lake or river stretch is engineered to hold. Example: land inside this line is legally meant to stay open for water, which is why its pooling return (400 sq yards/acre) is the smallest among patta categories. Encroachment land Land occupied or built on without a valid title, often riverbed or government land settled informally over time. Example: occupants here get 300 sq yards/acre — something, but the least of any category, reflecting their weaker legal claim. Transferable Development Rights (TDR) A certificate given to a landowner who surrenders land, letting them build extra floor area on a different plot they own, or sell that right to someone else (often a builder) instead of taking cash or a returned plot. Example: a buffer-zone owner here can choose TDR instead of the 800 sq-yard allotment. Land pooling vs. land acquisition Acquisition takes your land and pays fixed compensation under law; pooling takes your land TEMPORARILY, develops the whole area with roads and services, and gives you back a smaller, serviced plot from the same pooled land — the return ratio is set by whichever order governs that specific project, not by one universal rule. Example: today’s Musi ratios are one such project-specific pooling order, distinct from HMDA’s separate 60:40 one. 60:40 land-pooling ratio (HMDA) HMDA’s own standard scheme returns landowners roughly 60% of the value created (in practice, cited elsewhere as around 1,741 sq yards of developed plot per acre pooled), keeping 40% to sell and fund infrastructure. Example: this is the benchmark today’s Musi scheme is explicitly reported as NOT following. Multiple Use Zone A Master Plan land-use tag permitting a mix of residential, commercial and other uses on one parcel, rather than restricting it to a single use. Example: plots returned under this scheme carry this tag, which generally helps resale value and future construction flexibility. Master Plan A local or metropolitan authority’s official, legally-binding zoning map and rulebook, setting out what each area of land may be used for. Example: the "Multiple Use Zone" classification above is a Master Plan designation. Change-of-land-use (CLU) / land-use conversion charge A fee payable when a parcel’s officially recorded use (e.g. agricultural) is formally changed to another use (e.g. residential/commercial). Example: today’s scheme has the implementing entity, not the landowner, bear this charge on the plots handed back. Nala A natural or man-made storm-water drainage channel. Example: "nala charges" in this scheme relate to drainage-related costs on patta land, which the implementing entity is absorbing rather than passing to owners. Stamp duty A state tax paid on registering a property transaction, usually calculated as a percentage of the property’s market value. Example: Telangana’s normal combined stamp duty and registration charge runs close to 6% on an ordinary sale; this scheme fixes it at just 0.5% for plots returned to landowners — a real, quantifiable sweetener. 2026-10-01|ls-patta-2c: 2C patta explained: why assigned land drags buyers into CID cases Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: 2C Assigned Patta Explained: Why This Land Type Lands Buyers in CID Cases — 1acre.in Key Highlights Assigned patta is government WELFARE land with strings attached — strings that survive every deed registered after the original allotment. Restriction periods run 10–20 years by scheme — counted from the ALLOTMENT date, not from when the current seller acquired it. SC/ST-assigned land never loses its restriction. Buyers get pulled into CB-CID cases as often as sellers: registering a deed on restricted land counts as participation, intent or not. IPC 420, 465, 468 and 471 recur in these charge sheets — and 420 is NON-BAILABLE. 2C patta (converted-for-residential land) and assigned patta are DIFFERENT things — agents blur them, and that blur alone has put buyers in front of investigators. The patta’s remarks column and the A-Register hold everything you need — read both before any advance. What assigned patta actually is It reads like any other patta — survey number, name, extent, classification. The difference hides in a clause in the REMARKS section, or in the assignment order sitting behind the patta that sellers do not always show. Governments have allotted land to landless families, SC/ST beneficiaries, ex-servicemen and other eligible groups under welfare schemes — and the original assignment order carries the real terms: how long the beneficiary must hold, what the land may be used for, and whether government approval is needed before any sale. What the conditions mean in practice Restriction periods commonly run 10–20 years depending on the scheme — counted from the DATE OF ALLOTMENT, not from whenever the current seller took over. Violate them and the government cancels the patta and takes the land back — no warning, no compensation. The person who paid full market price is left with nothing, and on record the sale is treated as if it never legally happened. Why purchases turn into CID cases The script is always the same: a seller holds assigned land still inside its restriction period; the buyer is told the patta is clean or the condition “doesn’t apply anymore”; money moves, the deed registers. Then — sometimes years later — a neighbour complains or a revenue officer notices something during routine inspection. The Tahsildar orders an inquiry, confirms the violation, and the case moves to the police — often the CB-CID. The buyer’s registered deed is not a defence; it is EXHIBIT A. The criminal sections that get invoked IPC 420 — cheating by dishonest inducement, up to seven years, and NON-BAILABLE: arrest can precede a magistrate’s order. IPC 465 — forgery, where patta records were altered or a condition quietly omitted. IPC 468 — forgery for the purpose of cheating. IPC 471 — USING a forged document as genuine — the section that can reach a buyer who registered a deed without ever checking its underlying conditions. This is the lesson’s hardest truth: in assigned-land cases the buyer is treated as a participant, not merely a victim. 2C patta ≠ assigned patta 2C patta : agricultural land formally CONVERTED for residential use — its one condition (agricultural classification) already resolved through a conversion order. No welfare distribution behind it, no community restriction, no lock-in on sale. Assigned patta : welfare redistribution, with conditions on who may own, how long they must hold, and whether it can be sold at all. Agents in a hurry blur the two — and that blur alone has put buyers in front of investigators. If a seller says “2C”, verify it is a CONVERSION story, not an ASSIGNMENT story: the paper trail behind each is completely different. Example: A buyer is shown a “2C patta — fully converted, free to sell”. The A-Register extract tells another story: allotted 2011 under a housing scheme to an SC beneficiary — an assignment, restriction unexpired and, being SC-assigned, never expiring. The “conversion” framing was the con. One ₹50 counter application at the revenue office exposed it. How to verify before you pay ☐ Pull the LATEST patta/ownership record from the state portal. ☐ Get the A-REGISTER extract (or state equivalent) at the revenue office — it shows the original allotment date and scheme. ☐ Compute the restriction period from the ALLOTMENT date, not the seller’s purchase date. ☐ SC/ST-assigned? The restriction does not expire — check buyer eligibility before going one step further. ☐ Even past the window, some schemes require written Collector permission before registration — confirm. ☐ Review the ownership history: a pattern of quick, repeated transfers is exactly what CB-CID investigations flag. Quick answers (FAQ) Can assigned patta land be sold legally? Only where the scheme’s conditions allow — restriction expired, permissions obtained, or formal de-restriction granted. The non-alienation period? 10–20 years by scheme, from allotment; perpetual for SC/ST assignments. Why do BUYERS end up in cases? Because registering a deed on restricted land is treated as participation in the violation. If conditions are violated? Cancellation, resumption without compensation — plus the criminal exposure above. Bottom line This is the one land category where a mistake is not just money — it is a charge sheet. The remarks column and the A-Register cost minutes and rupees to read; read them before any advance, and walk away from any seller who resists the reading. For you: Deepens your assigned-land gate with the criminal dimension: in Telangana assembly work, any parcel whose chain touches a government grant gets the allotment-order + A-Register/Dharani-remarks check BEFORE the agreement — because for a professional developer the reputational cost of one CID summons exceeds any parcel’s margin. And police the vocabulary in your own market: brokers saying “converted” when the record says “assigned” are handing you their liability. 2026-10-01|ls-nri-repat: NRI buying land in India: rules and repatriation Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: NRI Buying Land in India: Rules and Repatriation — 1acre.in Key Highlights NRIs purchase residential and commercial property freely — no cap, no RBI approval. Agricultural land, plantations and farmhouses: barred without RBI permission, granted only in exceptional cases. The funding account — NRE/FCNR vs NRO — decides how much of the sale proceeds can later leave India. Two ceilings coexist: USD 1 million per year (general), and a LIFETIME cap of two residential properties for full repatriation of foreign-funded purchases. Inherited farmland can be kept — but sold only to a resident Indian. FEMA violations are punished for real: penalties can reach three times the amount. What NRI purchase covers under FEMA No single rule — it depends entirely on the land’s category. Residential and commercial: open. Agricultural, plantation, farmhouse: RBI-permission territory, rarely granted. OCI cardholders follow broadly the same lines. Definition — FEMA: the Foreign Exchange Management Act — the law governing what non-residents may hold in India and how money crosses the border. Its property rules now live in the Non-debt Instruments Rules, 2019. How the source of funds decides repatriation The question nobody asks until selling: where did the purchase money COME from? NRE/FCNR (foreign currency) funding: full repatriation of proceeds — but only for two residential properties in a lifetime without special approval. NRO funding or Indian income: repatriation capped at USD 1 million per financial year, whatever the property count. Bought while still a resident: the same 1-million-per-year route through an NRO account. The account choice at purchase becomes irreversible history at sale. Repatriating inherited property Allowed — within the same framework: documentary proof of inheritance, taxes settled, the annual limit observed. The paperwork order matters more than the principle. Why agricultural land is a special case NRIs cannot buy it directly; they CAN inherit it — and then may sell only to a resident Indian citizen, never to another NRI or foreigner. Even after a legitimate sale, repatriation follows the standard annual framework. Inherit-only, sell-to-residents-only, repatriate-within-caps: that layered fence is where NRI families stumble years later. How repatriation actually works, step by step 1. Sale proceeds land in an NRO account — the mandatory starting point. 2. File the income-tax return for the sale year. 3. A chartered accountant issues Form 15CB confirming capital-gains tax is paid. 4. Submit Form 15CA online with the sale deed and bank statements. 5. The bank verifies, converts, remits. Not one bank visit — a CA, a bank and the tax department all signing off; budget weeks, not days. Red flags Cash, or any channel outside normal banking — an outright FEMA violation; every rupee must move through banks. Skipped or botched 15CA/15CB filings — transfers block. Farmland bought without approval — regulatory action, penalties up to three times the amount, and directed disposal of the property. Repatriation limits by funding route How the property was funded What can leave India The cap that applies NRE / FCNR (foreign funds) Full sale proceeds Two residential properties per LIFETIME; beyond that, RBI approval NRO account / Indian income Proceeds via NRO USD 1 million per financial year, any property count Bought while a resident Proceeds via NRO USD 1 million per year Inherited property Proceeds via NRO USD 1 million per year + inheritance proof + tax clearance Foreign funding suits a buyer who will sell at most two properties in a lifetime. NRO-funded and inherited assets share the annual cap — spreading sales across financial years is the planning lever. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ The land’s category confirmed — residential/commercial open; agricultural/plantation closed. ☐ Clear records kept of the funding account for every purchase. ☐ NRO + 15CA/15CB machinery started early when a sale approaches. ☐ The annual USD 1 million cap tracked across same-year sales. ☐ A FEMA-qualified advisor before any transaction. Quick answers (FAQ) Can an NRI buy agricultural land? Not without rare RBI permission — inheritance and (from resident specified relatives) gift are the doors. Is there a time limit to repatriate? The practical clock is tax compliance and the annual cap — plan sale-year paperwork in advance. Does the two-property rule apply to everything? Only to full repatriation of foreign-funded RESIDENTIAL purchases; the annual cap governs the rest. Bottom line Consistent rules, unforgiving of shortcuts: category first, funding account second, documentation third. Getting all three right at purchase is cheap; correcting a FEMA violation after is not. For you: NRI buyers are a real slice of the plot market — the developer fluent in their constraints closes them faster. Keep an NRI closing pack (bank-routed trail, TDS guidance, PoA template, mutation help), and never sell anything smelling of farmland to an NRI, however willing.
